notes: \cpara{A recap of three earlier posts by title, then a taxonomy. The key term, ``proper belief,'' is defined only by pointing back to ``anticipation-controlling.'' The example of a proper but wrong belief is prayer for a sick baby. It is the first of four religious examples in the post's five paragraphs: prayer here, vestments and a skullcap in the next paragraph, ``the Islamic Way'' after that, and ``religious professing'' after that.}

\cpara{The post's definition, and it has no test. ``Belief as group identification'' is given a name and a borrowed metaphor, but nothing here, or later, says how to tell a belief worn for belonging from a belief held for reasons that one's group also holds. Every later example depends on that distinction. The idea is also old. Social psychology has studied how people define themselves through groups at least since Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory (1979). The post credits only Hanson's blog comment.}

\cpara{The post's only worked example, and it does not show what the post needs. The belief it picks, that the hijackers were cowards, is mostly a moral judgment. Moral judgments anticipate little experience, so on the post's scheme many of them, sincere or not, come out as improper belief. The example has trouble separating attire from conviction, which is what it was chosen to do.}

\clogic{``Undoubtedly,'' with no evidence. The post cites nothing the hijackers wrote or said. The one image it offers of their view comes from an American film about an alien invasion. A paragraph about seeing the world as the Enemy sees it describes the Enemy in Hollywood's terms.}
\clogic{A regional stereotype in place of evidence: no bar and no conversation are described.}
\cfact{The phrase echoes President Bush's address to Congress on 20 September 2001: ``They hate our freedoms.'' The post does not name the speaker.}

\cfact{Stated as an absolute, and the record is more mixed. The post's example is the official ``cowardly act'' line, and people did contradict it in public. Six days after the attacks Bill Maher said on ABC's \textsc{Politically Incorrect}: ``Staying in the airplane when it hits the building, say what you want about it, [it's] not cowardly.'' Susan Sontag wrote in \textsc{The New Yorker} (24 September 2001 issue): ``they were not cowards.'' Both were attacked for it; advertisers left Maher's show, which was cancelled in June 2002. The record supports a weaker claim: contradicting the official line had a price. The post states an absolute, cites none of the record, and supports the absolute with an imagined bar.}

\cpara{The thesis about passion rests on the author's ``impression,'' which is qualified three times in two sentences: ``may help explain,'' ``Or so I suspect,'' ``I confess I'm not an expert here.'' Then the qualifiers stop, and the impression becomes a flat statement about the inner lives of religious people: ``it's not the same fire they had as a child.'' No person, study or observation is cited. The claim also cannot fail. Any passionate believer can be described as someone whose ``desperation can be mistaken for passion.'' By the rent test of the author's own ``Making Beliefs Pay Rent,'' posted five days earlier, this belief floats.}

\cpara{The conclusion, in four sentences, none supported. ``People will die for it'' is asserted with no case. The mechanism is the post's actual claim: that passion for a tribe passes to the tribe's beliefs. Nothing shows it. The example chosen, cheering for a sports team, involves no belief at all, so it shows passion for a group and nothing about passion for beliefs.}

\cpara{A claim about the whole of American politics, and every analogous party system, put in a footnote and deferred to ``another time.'' ``Swindle'' implies someone is cheating the voters; the footnote names no one. ``False dilemma'' implies hidden alternatives; it names none.}
